performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
question: How does Fauré end a Requiem on a rising line and a shimmering organ?
intro: The last movement sets a text from the burial service for sopranos over a shimmering organ figure, muted strings and, later, a harp. Listen for the climax on “Jerusalem” and the voices’ return to “requiem”.

sections.label: Chorus angelorum
sections.mNote: a harp enters beneath the sopranos’ melody

sections.label: Aeternam habeas requiem
sections.mNote: every voice sings “requiem” as the music subsides

cues.title: An organ that shimmers
cues.text: The organ plays a continuous shimmer of rapid broken chords in D major while muted violins, violas and cellos hold long notes. The sopranos enter alone on “In paradisum” with a long rising line.
cues.evidence: Pages 114–115 of the score give the organ figure, the strings marked Sourdines and the soprano entry in the third bar. The report shows onset density of 4 to 7 per second throughout, consistent with continuous organ figuration, and D major as the local key estimate through the first 45 seconds (0.64 to 0.89).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A composer going deaf
cues.text: From 1903 Fauré’s hearing failed, in time to near-total deafness. He still became director of the Paris Conservatoire in 1905, although he had not studied there, and entered the Institut in 1909.
cues.evidence: IRCAM’s biography of Fauré gives the onset of hearing trouble in 1903, its progress to near-total deafness, his directorship from 1905 despite not having studied at the Conservatoire, and his entry to the Institut in 1909.

cues.title: Jerusalem, the loudest point
cues.text: Around 1:10 the tenors and basses, divided, join the sopranos on “Jerusalem” in a crescendo that reaches the movement’s loudest point near 1:15. The organ’s shimmer continues without a break.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −16.5 dB at 1:00 to −12.1 dB at 1:05, −10.7 dB at 1:10 and −4.9 dB at 1:15, the loudest window of the file; boundaries at 1:04 (0.94) and 1:18 (1.00). Page 119 of the score marks Div. Ten. and Div. Bass. pp with cresc.

cues.title: The harp enters
cues.text: After the climax subsides, near 1:40 a harp enters with rising semiquaver figures under the sopranos’ “Chorus angelorum te suscipiat” (“may the choir of angels receive you”). The strings keep their long muted notes.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −4.9 dB at 1:15 to −13.6 dB at 1:20 and −19.6 dB at 1:35, with a boundary at 1:34 (0.60). Page 121 of the score shows the harp’s first entry (“Harpes.”) with the sopranos’ dolce phrase.

cues.title: Played at his own funeral
cues.text: The Requiem in its full-orchestra version was performed at Fauré’s own funeral in 1924, a national funeral held at the Madeleine, where he had been choirmaster and organist.
cues.evidence: The History section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem says the full-orchestra Requiem was performed at his funeral. IRCAM’s biography gives the national funeral and his appointments at the Madeleine; this site’s Fauré biography places the funeral there.

cues.title: Every voice sings “requiem”
cues.text: From about 2:32 the voices reach “aeternam habeas requiem” (“may you have eternal rest”) and sing “requiem” one after another over the organ and harp. The crescendo of the previous minutes has peaked and now falls.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −6.0 dB at 2:20 to −15.3 dB at 2:30 and −20.0 dB at 2:40, with boundaries at 2:32 (0.86) and 2:40 (0.87). Pages 124–125 of the score mark cresc. and then the staggered pp “Re-” entries at letter E.

cues.title: A lullaby of death
cues.text: Fauré said someone had called his Requiem “a lullaby of death”, but that he saw death as “a happy deliverance, an aspiration towards happiness above”, not a painful passage.
cues.evidence: The History section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem quotes the interview in which Fauré gives this account; René Gagnaux’s Frémaux page prints the French of the passage.

transitions.title: Divided voices join the sopranos
transitions.how: For the first minute the sopranos sing alone over the organ’s shimmer, with muted strings holding long notes. At “Jerusalem” the tenors and basses enter, divided and pianissimo, and the voices crescendo together. The harmony thickens as voices are added, while the organ keeps its broken-chord figure through the crescendo; the rise in sound comes from the choir’s growth more than from any change in the accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Relative level rises from −16.5 dB at 1:00 to −12.1 dB at 1:05 and −4.9 dB at 1:15, with boundaries at 1:04 (0.94) and 1:18 (1.00). Pages 115–119 of the score show the soprano line alone until the divided tenor and bass entries at page 119.

transitions.title: The climax recedes and the harp enters
transitions.how: The “Jerusalem” climax falls away through a diminuendo at letter C, and the sopranos begin a new phrase, “Chorus angelorum te suscipiat”, marked dolce. A harp then enters with rising semiquaver figures, adding a new colour to the organ and muted strings. The second half of the text gets its own sound: the harp’s sparkle is heard from here to the end.
transitions.evidence: Relative level falls from −4.9 dB at 1:15 to −13.6 dB at 1:20 and −19.6 dB at 1:35, with a boundary at 1:34 (0.60). Pages 120–121 of the score give the dim. at letter C and the harp’s first entry.

transitions.title: A rising line towards “aeternam”
transitions.how: At letter D the sopranos begin “Et cum Lazaro quondam paupere” (“and with Lazarus, once a poor man”) over the organ and harp. The strings crescendo through the next page and the sopranos’ line climbs towards “aeternam”. The text moves from the angels to the poor man and from there to rest, and the level rises as it does.
transitions.evidence: Relative level rises from −15.2 dB at 2:10 to −10.6 dB at 2:15 and −6.0 dB at 2:20, with a boundary at 2:16 (0.79). Pages 123–124 of the score give letter D and the cresc. marks in the strings.

transitions.title: Every voice sings “requiem”
transitions.how: The crescendo peaks and falls at letter E as the sopranos reach “aeternam habeas requiem” and the other voices enter one after another on “requiem”, pianissimo. The organ’s shimmer and the harp continue, and the strings fall to long held notes. The last word of the Requiem’s text is sung by the whole choir, quietly, after the climb of the previous page.
transitions.evidence: Relative level falls from −15.3 dB at 2:30 to −20.0 dB at 2:40, with boundaries at 2:32 (0.86) and 2:40 (0.87). Pages 125–127 of the score show the staggered pp “Re-” entries at letter E and the continuing organ and harp figures.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: VII. In paradisum, printed pp. 114–128. The strings are marked “Sourdines” (muted). The wind, brass and timpani staves are empty throughout. Entries are set from the page layout and the report’s boundaries.

timeline.note: The organ’s shimmering broken chords and muted strings accompany the sopranos’ rising line.
Divided tenors and basses join on Jerusalem, and the double basses enter pianissimo.
A harp enters with rising semiquavers under Chorus angelorum and stays to the end; the double basses rest.
The double basses return near the end of the page for the crescendo into letter E.
The voices sing requiem in turn, pianissimo; strings hold long notes while organ and harp continue their figures.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.27 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 2, track 3 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+50 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.44 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: A church organist who made the French song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; piano with Camille Saint-Saëns
Madeleine: choirmaster 1877–96, organist 1896–1905 · Paris Conservatoire: composition professor 1896–1905, director 1905–20
Mélodies, piano music, chamber music, Requiem, the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
Fauré learned his trade in a school for church musicians. His father was a schoolmaster in the Ariège; at nine, Gabriel was sent to Louis Niedermeyer’s recently founded school in Paris, where plainchant, Renaissance polyphony, organ playing and counterpoint belonged to the ordinary curriculum. The education matters to the harmony. A melody can cadence in minor with an unsharpened seventh degree; a chord can emerge from the independent movement of voices. These possibilities were practical knowledge before they became a recognisable Fauré style.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class and introduced the pupils to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Teacher and pupil remained friends for more than sixty years. Fauré’s graduation work, the Cantique de Jean Racine of 1865, already joins the two educations: a flowing keyboard accompaniment beneath a choral texture whose entries are controlled by contrapuntal discipline. Its French text is Racine’s paraphrase of a Latin hymn. The bass supports long phrases that carry the upper voices across the bar-lines.
